title: Freelance Client Boundaries Kit
description: Stop answering client messages at 10pm without losing the client. A 12-question boundaries audit, a fill-in working hours and communication policy with a finished example, 14 scripts and emails for late-night messages, scattered channels, quick calls and unpaid favours, an urgent-request triage with emergency rate maths, a tool setup checklist, six paste-ready auto-replies and a boundary log.

files.01-boundaries-audit.md:
# 1. Boundaries Audit

Answer each question about the **last four weeks**, not a typical month you wish you'd had. Score each one 0, 1 or 2.

- **0** = this is a real problem right now
- **1** = sometimes a problem
- **2** = fine, this is under control

## The 12 questions

### Hours and availability

1. **Do clients know your working hours?** Would every active client give the same answer if asked?
   0 = no one knows · 1 = some know, or it's vague · 2 = written down and shared

2. **How often did you reply to a client outside your working hours?**
   0 = most days · 1 = once or twice a week · 2 = rarely, and by choice

3. **Do you check client messages before starting work or after finishing?**
   0 = every day · 1 = a few times a week · 2 = almost never

4. **Have you taken a full day off (no client messages at all) in the last four weeks?**
   0 = no · 1 = yes, but I checked "just once" · 2 = yes, fully off

### Channels

5. **How many channels do clients use to reach you?** (email, chat apps, text, phone, voice notes, project tools, social media)
   0 = four or more · 1 = two or three · 2 = one main channel, one backup

6. **Have you missed or nearly missed a request because it came in on an unexpected channel?**
   0 = yes, more than once · 1 = once · 2 = no

7. **Does any client contact you on a personal number or personal social account?**
   0 = yes, regularly · 1 = occasionally · 2 = no

### Calls and meetings

8. **Are calls booked in advance with a clear length and agenda?**
   0 = most calls are unplanned · 1 = about half · 2 = nearly all

9. **How often did a "quick call" run more than twice as long as expected?**
   0 = most times · 1 = sometimes · 2 = rarely

### Scope and urgency

10. **How many small unbilled extras did you do in the last four weeks?** (tweaks, favours, "while you're in there")
    0 = more than five · 1 = two to five · 2 = one or none

11. **How often was something labelled "urgent" that wasn't?**
    0 = often · 1 = sometimes · 2 = rarely, or I have a clear definition of urgent

12. **Do you charge more for out-of-hours or rush work?**
    0 = never, and I do it often · 1 = sometimes, or I'm unsure how · 2 = yes, and clients know in advance

## Scoring

| Total | What it means | Where to start |
|---|---|---|
| 0-8 | Your clients set your hours. This is the fast road to burnout. | Write your policy (file 02) this week and send the reset email (file 03, script 1) to your two most demanding clients. |
| 9-16 | Some structure, but it leaks under pressure. | Fix your three lowest-scoring questions first. Most people at this level gain the most from channels and urgency. |
| 17-24 | Solid. Your job is to keep it that way as you grow. | Add the policy to your onboarding and review the boundary log monthly. |

## Find your three priorities

Write your three lowest-scoring questions here. If several are tied, pick the ones that cost you the most sleep or the most money.

| Priority | Question number | What's happening now | What I want instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | |
| 2 | | | |
| 3 | | | |

### Example

| Priority | Question number | What's happening now | What I want instead |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 5 | Clients use email, chat, text and voice notes. I lose track of requests. | All requests by email. Chat only for quick questions on project days. |
| 2 | 3 | I check messages in bed before 7am. | First check at 9:30am after I've done an hour of focused work. |
| 3 | 10 | About eight small unbilled favours a month. | Anything over 15 minutes gets quoted or added to the next invoice. |

## Why each area matters

- **Hours.** If you don't state hours, clients assume you're always available. Most aren't being rude; they just don't know.
- **Channels.** Every extra channel is one more place to check and one more place to miss something. One main channel makes you faster and more reliable, not less.
- **Calls.** Unplanned calls break focus. Ten minutes on the phone can cost you 40 minutes of deep work.
- **Scope and urgency.** Unbilled favours and false emergencies quietly lower your hourly rate. Clear rules protect your income as well as your evenings.

Run this audit again in three months and compare your score.
files.02-working-policy.md:
# 2. Your "How We Work Together" Page

This is a short, friendly page you give every client at the start of a project. It answers the questions clients would otherwise ask at the worst moment: When are you around? How fast will you reply? What if something breaks on a Saturday?

Keep it to one page. Paste it into your welcome email, your onboarding document or your proposal.

## Tips before you write

- **Write it for the client, not against them.** Explain how it helps them: faster answers, nothing lost, better work.
- **Promise what you can keep on your worst week,** not your best. It's better to promise a one-day reply and beat it than to promise one hour and miss it.
- **Use your real time zone** and say it out loud if you work with clients elsewhere.
- **Give one clear emergency route,** and say what it costs if it's outside hours.

## Template

Copy everything between the lines and replace the parts in [square brackets].

---

**How we'll work together**

Thanks for working with me. Here's how I run my week so you always know when and how to reach me.

**My working hours**
I work [days], [start time] to [end time] ([time zone]). I'm not available on [days or public holidays]. I'll always tell you about time off at least [number] weeks ahead.

**How to reach me**
Please send requests and feedback by [main channel]. That way nothing gets lost and everything stays in one place. For quick questions during a working day, [backup channel] is fine. I don't use [channels you don't use, e.g. text messages or social media] for work.

**How quickly I'll reply**
I reply to messages within [time, e.g. one working day], usually sooner. Messages sent after [time] or on [days off] will be answered the next working day.

**Calls**
I'm happy to talk. Please book a call using [how they book] so we both have time to prepare. Calls are usually [length] minutes. If something needs a quick chat, let me know and I'll suggest a time that day or the next.

**Urgent issues**
"Urgent" means [your definition, e.g. your live website is down or a deadline you can't move is at risk]. If that happens, [what to do, e.g. send an email with URGENT in the subject line and a text to my work number]. I'll respond within [time] during working hours. Out-of-hours emergency help is [available / available by arrangement / not available], charged at [rate or "my rush rate"].

**Small requests and extras**
I'm glad to help with small things. Anything that takes more than [number] minutes or sits outside the agreed scope, I'll quote first so you're never surprised by an invoice.

**Focus time**
I block out time for focused work, so I may not reply instantly during the day. That's how your project gets my full attention.

Thanks, I'm looking forward to working together.

[Your name]

---

## Finished example

Here's how one freelance web designer filled it in.

---

**How we'll work together**

Thanks for working with me. Here's how I run my week so you always know when and how to reach me.

**My working hours**
I work Monday to Thursday, 9am to 5:30pm (UK time). Fridays are for my own admin and training, and I'm not available on weekends or UK bank holidays. I'll always tell you about time off at least three weeks ahead.

**How to reach me**
Please send requests and feedback by email. That way nothing gets lost and everything stays in one place. During an active build week, our shared project board is fine for quick questions. I don't use text messages or social media for client work.

**How quickly I'll reply**
I reply to emails within one working day, usually the same afternoon. Emails sent after 5:30pm or on Friday to Sunday will be answered the next working day.

**Calls**
I'm happy to talk. Please book a call using the scheduling link in my email signature, so we both have time to prepare. Calls are usually 30 minutes. If something needs a quick chat, let me know and I'll suggest a time that day or the next.

**Urgent issues**
"Urgent" means your live website is down, a form has stopped sending, or there's a security problem. If that happens, email me with URGENT in the subject and text my work number. I'll respond within two hours during working hours. Out of hours, I'll do my best to respond the same evening, and any emergency work outside my hours is charged at 1.5 times my hourly rate, with a one-hour minimum.

**Small requests and extras**
I'm glad to help with small things. Anything that takes more than 20 minutes or sits outside the agreed scope, I'll quote first so you're never surprised by an invoice.

**Focus time**
I block out mornings for design and development work, so I usually reply to emails after midday. That's how your project gets my full attention.

Thanks, I'm looking forward to working together.

Sam

---

## Where to put it

- **New clients:** attach it to your welcome email and mention it on your kick-off call. Say: "There's a one-page guide to how I work. It'll save us both time."
- **Proposals:** add a short "Working hours and communication" section with the three key lines: hours, main channel, reply time.
- **Email signature:** one line, such as "Working hours: Mon-Thu, 9-5:30 UK. I reply within one working day."
- **Existing clients:** use the reset email in file 03.

## Checklist

- [ ] Working days and hours, with time zone
- [ ] Days off and how much notice you give for holidays
- [ ] One main channel, at most one backup
- [ ] Reply time you can keep on a bad week
- [ ] How to book calls and how long they are
- [ ] Definition of urgent, plus the emergency route
- [ ] Out-of-hours rate or "not available"
- [ ] The small-request threshold in minutes
- [ ] Fits on one page
files.03-scripts-and-emails.md:
# 3. Scripts and Emails

Fourteen replies for the moments when boundaries get tested. Each one follows the same pattern:

1. **Acknowledge** the request, so the client feels heard.
2. **State** what you'll do and when.
3. **Offer** a route forward, so it never feels like a closed door.

Adapt the wording to sound like you. Keep them short. A long explanation sounds defensive; a short one sounds settled.

---

## Setting up and resetting

### Script 1: Reset email for an existing client

Use this when a client has got used to reaching you at any time, and you want to change that without drama. Send it at a calm moment, not straight after a late-night message.

> **Subject:** A quick update on how I'm organising my week
>
> Hi [Name],
>
> I'm making a few changes to how I organise my week so I can give every project more focused time. Nothing changes about the work itself. I just wanted you to know what to expect from [date].
>
> - My working hours are [days, times, time zone].
> - The best way to reach me is [main channel]. I reply within [reply time].
> - For anything urgent (like [example]), [emergency route].
>
> I've attached a one-page guide with the details. If anything in it doesn't work for your team, just tell me and we'll figure it out.
>
> Thanks, as always, for being great to work with.
>
> [Your name]

**Why it works:** It's framed around better work for them, it gives a start date, and it invites them to raise concerns instead of resenting the change.

### Script 2: Mentioning your hours on a kick-off call

> "Before we dive in, a quick note on how I work. I'm around [days and hours], and email is the best way to reach me. I reply within [time]. If something's truly urgent, [route]. I've put it all in a one-page guide I'll send after this call. Does that work for how your team operates?"

---

## Out-of-hours messages

### Script 3: The late-evening or weekend message (non-urgent)

Often the best reply is no reply until your next working morning. If you do want to acknowledge it, schedule this to send at the start of your next working day:

> Hi [Name], thanks for this. I've added it to my list and will have [the answer / an update] for you by [time or day].

Don't apologise for not replying sooner. You were outside your hours; nothing went wrong.

### Script 4: A client who has noticed you're slower to reply

> Hi [Name], you're right that I'm replying a bit later than before. I've started blocking out focused time for project work, so I now reply to messages [when]. If anything ever needs a faster answer, [emergency route] will always reach me.

### Script 5: Messages to your personal number or account

> Hi [Name], thanks for the message. I keep this number for personal use, so I might miss things sent here. Could you send this to [work channel]? That way it goes straight into my project list and won't get lost.

If it happens again, reply only on the work channel: "Picked up your message. Replying here so it's all in one place."

---

## Channels

### Script 6: Requests scattered across chat, text and voice notes

> Hi [Name], quick favour to keep things running smoothly. Could we keep requests and feedback in [main channel]? I've had a few things come in across different apps, and I'd hate to miss something important. I'll keep everything in one thread so it's easy to find later.

### Script 7: A voice note with a detailed request

> Thanks for the voice note. To make sure I get this exactly right, I've written down what I heard:
>
> 1. [Point]
> 2. [Point]
>
> Could you confirm this is correct, or correct anything I've missed? I'll start as soon as you reply.

Turning it into text protects you both. It also gently teaches that written requests move faster.

---

## Calls

### Script 8: "Can you jump on a quick call?"

> Happy to talk. I'm in focused work right now, but I can do [two specific times]. Would either work? If you send me a line or two on what it's about, I'll come prepared and we can keep it short.

### Script 9: Keeping a call to time

At the start: "I've got us down for 30 minutes. What's the most important thing to cover?"

Five minutes before the end: "We've got five minutes left. Let's agree the next steps, and I'll send a summary today."

If it needs longer: "This needs more time than we've got. Shall we book another 30 minutes, or would it help if I wrote up some options for you to look at first?"

---

## Scope and favours

### Script 10: The "quick favour" that isn't quick

> Happy to help with this. It's outside what we agreed for the project, and I estimate it at about [time]. I can do it for [price], and fit it in by [date]. Shall I go ahead?

### Script 11: A small favour you're happy to do once

If you choose to do it free, say so, so it doesn't become expected:

> Done. This one's on me, as it was quick. For future changes like this, I'll send a short quote first so you always know where you stand.

---

## Urgency

### Script 12: "Urgent!" that isn't urgent

> Thanks for flagging this. I can see why it's frustrating. It isn't something that will stop [the site / the launch / sales] working, so I've put it at the top of my list for [next working day / time]. If anything changes and it starts affecting [important thing], tell me and I'll look sooner.

### Script 13: A real out-of-hours emergency

> I've seen your message and I'm looking at it now. As this is outside my working hours, it'll be billed at my emergency rate of [rate], as set out in our working guide. I'll update you within [time].

If you can't help: "I'm not available tonight, but I'll be on this first thing at [time]. In the meantime, [one practical step the client can take, if there is one]."

---

## When a boundary keeps being crossed

### Script 14: The direct conversation

Use this when a client has had the policy, had a reminder or two, and nothing has changed. Have this conversation on a call, then confirm in writing.

> "I want to raise something openly, because I value working with you. Over the last [period], a lot of requests have come in [late at night / by text / as urgent]. I'm finding it hard to give your project my best work when I'm reacting to messages around the clock. Could we agree to [specific change]? If your team really needs evening cover, I can offer that as a paid add-on at [price]. What would work best for you?"

Then follow up:

> Thanks for talking this through today. As agreed: [summary of change]. I'll start with that from [date].

If nothing changes after this, it's a sign this client may not be a long-term fit. That's a business decision, not a failure.

---

## Phrases to avoid, and what to say instead

| Instead of | Try |
|---|---|
| "Sorry for the slow reply!" | "Thanks for your patience." (or nothing) |
| "I know this is annoying, but..." | "So I can do my best work, ..." |
| "I'm really overwhelmed right now." | "I can fit this in by [date]." |
| "I'm not allowed to work weekends." | "I don't work weekends. I'll pick this up on Monday." |
| "Is it okay if I reply tomorrow?" | "I'll reply tomorrow by midday." |
| "It's just a tiny thing, no charge." (every time) | "This one's on me. Next time I'll quote first." |
files.04-urgent-requests.md:
# 4. Handling Urgent Requests

Most boundary problems come down to one word: urgent. If you don't define it, the client will, and to a busy client almost everything feels urgent.

## Step 1: Write your definition

A good definition is specific, short and tied to real harm. Fill this in:

> For my clients, "urgent" means: [something is broken or at risk that will cost the client money, customers or a deadline that can't move] **and** [it can't wait until my next working morning].

### Examples by type of freelancer

| Freelancer | Urgent | Not urgent |
|---|---|---|
| Web designer or developer | Site down, checkout broken, security problem | Colour tweak, new page, typo on an old blog post |
| Copywriter or content writer | Factual error in a live campaign, legal team pulled a claim before a launch | New headline ideas, "can you look at this when you can?" |
| Social media manager | Wrong post went live, a negative post is spreading fast | Next month's calendar, new hashtag ideas |
| Bookkeeper or virtual assistant | Payroll or payment deadline today with missing information | Monthly reports, filing that's due next week |
| Designer | Printer deadline today and the file was rejected | Logo variations, new social graphics |
| Video editor | Broadcast or launch deadline today and the file won't export | Small trims, music swap on a draft |

## Step 2: Triage any out-of-hours request in under a minute

Ask yourself three questions, in order.

**1. Is it urgent by my definition?**
- No → it waits until your next working day. Optionally schedule a short acknowledgement for the morning (file 03, script 3).
- Yes → go to question 2.

**2. Have I offered out-of-hours cover to this client?**
- No → reply with what you can do and when (file 03, script 13, second version). Suggest any step they can take themselves.
- Yes → go to question 3.

**3. Can I handle it right now, without risk to my health, family or other commitments?**
- Yes → handle it, tell the client the emergency rate applies, and log it.
- No → tell them when you can start, and stick to it.

You don't owe anyone an instant reply outside your hours. You do owe clear communication about when you'll act.

## Step 3: Decide your out-of-hours option

Pick one of these and put it in your working policy.

### Option A: Not available

Best for: freelancers with families, health needs or other jobs, and for services where nothing truly breaks overnight.

> "I'm not available outside my working hours. For true emergencies I'll respond at the start of my next working day."

### Option B: Best effort, charged

Best for: most freelancers whose work is live (websites, campaigns, ads).

> "Out of hours, I'll respond to true emergencies when I can, usually the same evening. Emergency work outside my hours is charged at [1.5x / 2x] my hourly rate, with a [one-hour] minimum."

### Option C: Paid cover

Best for: clients who need someone on call, such as online shops during sales periods or businesses with big launches.

> "If you need guaranteed evening or weekend cover, I offer on-call support for [price] per [week / month], with a response within [time]. Any work during cover is billed at my standard rate."

A paid cover option can turn a boundary problem into a small extra income stream. Clients who truly need cover will usually pay for it; clients who don't will stop sending late-night "urgent" messages.

## Setting an emergency rate

There's no single right number, but here's a simple way to think about it:

- **1.5x your hourly rate** is a common middle ground for evening work.
- **2x** is common for weekends, public holidays and very short notice.
- **A minimum charge** (often one hour) stops a 5-minute fix from costing you a whole evening of focus for a tiny fee.

### Worked example

Priya charges $60 an hour. Her policy says out-of-hours emergencies are 1.5x with a one-hour minimum.

A client's checkout stops working on a Saturday morning. Priya spends 40 minutes fixing it.

- Emergency rate: $60 x 1.5 = $90 an hour
- Time: 40 minutes, but one-hour minimum applies
- Charge: $90

She sends a short email: "Fixed and tested. The cause was [cause]. As this was outside my working hours, it's billed at my emergency rate ($90, one-hour minimum). It'll be on your next invoice."

The client is relieved, not annoyed, because it was agreed in advance.

## Step 4: Track it

Log every out-of-hours request in `boundary-log.csv`, even ones you didn't act on. After a month you'll see:

- Which clients cause most of the pressure
- Which channel it comes through
- How many were truly urgent by your definition

If one client causes most of the out-of-hours requests, that's a conversation (file 03, script 14) or a price change, not a personal failing.
files.05-setup-checklist.md:
# 5. Setup Checklist

A policy only works if your tools back it up. This checklist works with any email, chat or phone app. Most have these settings, though they may use different names.

Set aside 20 minutes. Tick each item as you go.

## Notifications

- [ ] **Turn off work notifications outside your hours.** Use your phone's focus, quiet or do-not-disturb schedule. Set it to match the hours in your policy.
- [ ] **Allow one emergency exception.** If you offer emergency cover, let calls or messages from your work number or a short list of key contacts through. Nothing else.
- [ ] **Remove work email badges from your home screen,** or move work apps off the first screen. If you can't see the number, you won't feel the pull.
- [ ] **Turn off sounds for chat apps during focus time.** Check them at set times instead (see "Message windows" below).

## Channels

- [ ] **Pick one main channel** (usually email) and one backup at most. Write them in your policy.
- [ ] **Set up an email signature line** with your hours and reply time. Example: "Working hours: Mon-Thu, 9-5:30 UK time. I reply within one working day."
- [ ] **Set a status on chat tools** showing your hours. Use the status messages in `auto-replies.txt`.
- [ ] **Consider a separate work number.** Many phones support two numbers, or you can use a low-cost second line. This makes "off" a real thing.
- [ ] **Create a filter or folder per client** so requests land in one place you can review in a batch.

## Auto-replies

- [ ] **Out-of-hours auto-reply** for email, if your app supports schedules. Use message 1 or 2 in `auto-replies.txt`.
- [ ] **Holiday auto-reply** ready to switch on (message 4).
- [ ] **Focus-time auto-reply** if you block whole mornings or days (message 3).

Don't set an auto-reply to fire on every single email all day. That annoys clients. Use it only outside hours, on days off, or during long focus blocks.

## Message windows

Instead of reacting all day, check messages at set times. A common pattern:

| Time | What to do |
|---|---|
| Start of day (after your first focus block) | Read everything, reply to quick items, add bigger ones to your task list |
| Early afternoon | Second check; send replies and updates |
| End of day | Final check; send anything promised "today"; schedule morning replies |

Write your windows here:

| Window | Time |
|---|---|
| 1 | |
| 2 | |
| 3 | |

## Calendar

- [ ] **Block focus time** on your calendar as busy, so booking tools don't offer it.
- [ ] **Set a booking tool or a list of call slots** with fixed lengths (15, 30 or 45 minutes).
- [ ] **Add buffer time** of 10-15 minutes after calls, so one late call doesn't knock out your whole afternoon.
- [ ] **Put holidays in your calendar now,** and tell clients at least two to three weeks ahead.

## Scheduled sending

- [ ] **Use "send later"** when you choose to work in the evening. Write the reply at 9pm, schedule it for 9am. Clients see your working hours, not your evenings.

## The weekly 10-minute check

Every Friday (or your last working day), spend 10 minutes on this:

1. Did I reply outside my hours this week? How many times, and why?
2. Did any client use a channel I don't use for work?
3. Did any unbilled extras slip through? Add them to the next invoice or note them for next time.
4. Is there one boundary I need to restate next week? Pick the script now.
5. Update `boundary-log.csv`.

## Signs it's working

After two to four weeks, you should notice:

- Fewer messages outside your hours, because clients have adjusted
- Requests arriving in one place
- Calls that start and end on time
- More extras turning into paid work
- Evenings and weekends that feel like your own again

If it isn't working with one particular client, use script 14 in file 03.
files.README.md:
# Freelance Client Boundaries Kit

Stop answering client messages at 10pm without losing the client. This kit helps you decide when you work, how clients reach you and what counts as urgent. You then write it down once and say it the same calm way every time.

Plan on about 90 minutes to set up. After that, it mostly runs itself.

## Who this is for

You're a freelancer, and some of these sound familiar:

- You check messages first thing in the morning and last thing at night "just in case".
- A client sends work requests by text, chat, email and voice notes, and you lose track.
- "Quick calls" turn into an hour, and they're never on your calendar.
- Small favours keep piling up and never get billed.
- You feel guilty when you don't reply within minutes.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| 01-boundaries-audit.md | A 12-question audit that shows where your time is leaking, with scoring |
| 02-working-policy.md | A fill-in "How we work together" page for clients, plus a finished example |
| 03-scripts-and-emails.md | Ready replies for 14 common situations, from late-night messages to unpaid "quick favours" |
| 04-urgent-requests.md | How to define "urgent", a simple triage for out-of-hours requests, and an emergency cover option |
| 05-setup-checklist.md | Practical setup: notification schedules, auto-replies, channels and a weekly 10-minute check |
| auto-replies.txt | Six auto-reply and status messages you can paste straight into your email and chat apps |
| boundary-log.csv | A simple log to spot which clients and channels cause the most out-of-hours pressure |

## How to use it

1. **Audit (20 minutes).** Answer the 12 questions in `01-boundaries-audit.md`. Note your three lowest-scoring areas. Those are your priorities.
2. **Write your policy (30 minutes).** Fill in the template in `02-working-policy.md`. Use the finished example if you get stuck. Keep it to one page.
3. **Set up your tools (20 minutes).** Work through `05-setup-checklist.md` and paste in messages from `auto-replies.txt`.
4. **Tell your clients (20 minutes).** New clients get the policy with your welcome pack. For existing clients, use the "reset" email in `03-scripts-and-emails.md`.
5. **Hold the line (ongoing).** When something comes up, find the matching script, adapt it, and log it in `boundary-log.csv`. Review the log once a month.

## Ground rules

- **Boundaries are about access, not attitude.** You aren't telling clients what to do. You're telling them when and how you'll respond. Keep your tone warm and plain.
- **Say it before you need it.** A policy shared at the start of a project feels professional. The same words in the middle of a tense week can feel like a complaint.
- **Be consistent.** If you reply at 11pm once, clients learn that 11pm works. You don't need to be rigid, but exceptions should be your choice, not a habit.
- **Offer a real route for real emergencies.** Clients relax about boundaries when they know true emergencies will still get handled.
- **Bill for what you give.** Out-of-hours work and extra calls have value. The scripts here show how to say so without awkwardness.

This kit gives general business guidance, not legal advice. If you want availability terms written into a contract, have your contract reviewed by a qualified professional where you work.
files.auto-replies.txt:
AUTO-REPLIES AND STATUS MESSAGES
Replace everything in [square brackets]. Keep them short and warm.

----------------------------------------
1. OUT-OF-HOURS EMAIL AUTO-REPLY (standard)
----------------------------------------
Subject: Thanks for your message

Hi,

Thanks for getting in touch. My working hours are [days], [start]-[end] ([time zone]), so I'll reply on my next working day.

If this is a true emergency for a current project (for example, [your urgent example]), please [emergency route].

Thanks,
[Your name]

----------------------------------------
2. OUT-OF-HOURS EMAIL AUTO-REPLY (short)
----------------------------------------
Thanks for your email. I'm outside my working hours right now and will reply by [time] on my next working day.

[Your name]

----------------------------------------
3. FOCUS-TIME AUTO-REPLY (for long focus blocks or whole focus days)
